questions.title: Minimum Window Substring — smallest substring in A containing all chars of B
questions.body:
Given two strings s and t, return the minimum window substring of s such that every character in t (including duplicates) is included in the window. If no such substring exists, return "".

Example 1
Input: s = "ADOBECODEBANC", t = "ABC"
Output: "BANC"
Explanation: "BANC" is the shortest substring of s that contains A, B, and C.
Example 2
Input: s = "a", t = "aa"
Output: ""
Explanation: t needs two a's, but s has only one.

Constraints

  • 1 <= s.length, t.length <= 10^5
  • s and t consist of English letters.
questions.answer:
Problem: Find the smallest substring of A that contains every character of B (with multiplicity).

Idea — sliding window + two frequency maps:

  1. Build need: counts of chars required from B. Track missing = how many chars still needed.
  2. Expand right. When you cover a needed char, decrement missing.
  3. While the window is valid (missing == 0), shrink left to minimise length and record the best [L,R].
  4. When shrinking removes a needed char, increment missing again.

Why it works: every time the window becomes valid you have a candidate; shrinking finds the leftmost start for that right endpoint. Over all right endpoints you cover the global minimum.

Complexity: O(|A| + |B|) time, O(charset) space. Edge cases: empty B; B longer than A; duplicate chars in B; no valid window → return empty.

Interview tip: dry-run on A="ADOBECODEBANC", B="ABC". Mention Java is often required at MMT even if you sketch C++.

solutions.label: C++

questions.source: Reported: SDE-2 GFG 2021, MMT Campus, Code360 2022
questions.hint: Sliding window with two frequency maps. Expand right, shrink left when valid. Track best window.

questions.title: Subarray with Sum Zero — find any subarray whose sum = 0
questions.body:
Given an integer array nums, return any contiguous subarray whose elements sum to 0. If none exists, return an empty array. (Returning the start and end indices is also acceptable — state which you return.)

Example 1
Input: nums = [1, 2, -3, 4, -1]
Output: [1, 2, -3]
Explanation: 1 + 2 + (-3) = 0. Indices [0, 2] are also a valid answer.
Example 2
Input: nums = [1, 2, 3]
Output: []
Explanation: No contiguous subarray sums to 0.

Constraints

  • 1 <= nums.length <= 10^5
  • -10^9 <= nums[i] <= 10^9
questions.answer:
Problem: Detect any contiguous subarray whose sum is 0 (or return its indices).

Idea — prefix sums + HashMap: let pref[i] = a[0]+…+a[i]. If pref[j] == pref[i-1], then a[i..j] sums to 0. Also if pref[j] == 0, a[0..j] works.

  1. Scan left→right maintaining running sum s.
  2. Store first index where each prefix appeared (or a set if you only need yes/no).
  3. On seeing a repeated prefix (or 0), you found a zero-sum subarray.

Complexity: O(N) time, O(N) space. Edge cases: single 0; negatives; multiple answers — any is fine unless asked for longest/shortest.

solutions.label: C++

questions.hint: Approach: Prefix sum + HashMap. If same prefix sum appears twice, the subarray between them sums to 0.

questions.title: Merge K Sorted Arrays / Linked Lists
questions.body:
You are given an array of k linked lists, each sorted in ascending order. Merge all the lists into one sorted linked list and return it.

Example 1
Input: lists = [[1,4,5],[1,3,4],[2,6]]
Output: [1,1,2,3,4,4,5,6]
Example 2
Input: lists = []
Output: []

Input: lists = [[]]
Output: []

Constraints

  • 0 <= k <= 10^4
  • 0 <= total nodes <= 10^4
  • -10^4 <= Node.val <= 10^4
  • Each list is sorted ascending.
questions.answer:
Problem: Merge K sorted linked lists into one sorted list.

Idea — min-heap of size K:

  1. Push the head of each non-empty list into a min-heap keyed by node value.
  2. Repeatedly pop the smallest node, append to the result, and push that node’s next if any.

Why heap: you always need the global minimum among K frontiers — heap gives O(log K) per extract.

Complexity: O(N log K) time for N total nodes, O(K) heap space. Pitfalls: null lists in the input array; define a proper ListNode constructor (dummy head pattern).

Alternatives: pairwise merge (like merge-sort) also O(N log K); divide-and-conquer merging of lists.

solutions.label: C++

questions.source: Reported: SDE-2 GFG 2021, SDE-1 Naukri Aug 2024
questions.hint: Min-heap of size K — always extract minimum, push next from same list.

questions.title: Jump Game II — minimum number of jumps (+ return jump indexes)
questions.body:
You are given a 0-indexed array of integers nums of length n. You start at index 0. Each element nums[i] is the maximum forward jump length from index i. Return the minimum number of jumps to reach index n - 1. The test cases are generated so you can always reach the last index. Follow-up: also return one sequence of jump indexes.

Example 1
Input: nums = [2,3,1,1,4]
Output: 2
Explanation: Jump 1 step from index 0 to 1, then 3 steps to the last index.
Example 2
Input: nums = [2,3,0,1,4]
Output: 2
Explanation: Jump from index 0 to 1, then from 1 to 4.

Constraints

  • 1 <= nums.length <= 10^4
  • 0 <= nums[i] <= 1000
questions.answer:
Problem: Minimum jumps to reach the last index (Jump Game II). Optionally reconstruct jump positions.

Idea — greedy BFS layers: treat indices reachable with the same jump count as a “layer”.

  1. Maintain curEnd (end of current jump’s reach) and farthest (furthest you can reach while scanning the layer).
  2. When i == curEnd, you must take another jump: jumps++, set curEnd = farthest.

Path variant: while scanning each layer, record the first parent that reaches each new index; reconstruct from n-1 back to 0. Cap reach at n-1 to avoid out-of-bounds.

Complexity: O(N) time / O(1) space for count; O(N) space for path. Edge: already at end (n≤1); unreachable array (path returns empty).

solutions.label: C++

questions.source: Reported: SSE-2 LeetCode Discuss Nov 2023, CodingKaro
questions.hint: Greedy: track current range end and furthest reachable. When pointer hits current end, increment jump count.

questions.title: Merge Overlapping Intervals
questions.body:
Given an array of intervals where intervals[i] = [starti, endi], merge all overlapping intervals and return an array of the non-overlapping intervals that cover all the intervals in the input. Touching endpoints (end == next start) should be merged.

Example 1
Input: intervals = [[1,3],[2,6],[8,10],[15,18]]
Output: [[1,6],[8,10],[15,18]]
Explanation: [1,3] and [2,6] overlap, so they merge into [1,6].
Example 2
Input: intervals = [[1,4],[4,5]]
Output: [[1,5]]

Constraints

  • 1 <= intervals.length <= 10^4
  • intervals[i].length == 2
  • 0 <= starti <= endi <= 10^4
questions.answer:
Problem: Merge all overlapping intervals.

Idea:

  1. Sort by start time.
  2. Scan: if current start ≤ last merged end, extend end = max(end, current.end); else push a new interval.

Why sort: after sorting, overlaps can only involve the previous interval in the result — one linear pass.

Complexity: O(N log N) sort + O(N). Edge: touching intervals [1,2][2,3] — decide if inclusive merge (usually yes); empty input; single interval.

solutions.label: C++

questions.hint: Sort intervals by start. Scan and merge when current.start <= last.end; else push new interval.

questions.title: Multiply Two Large Integers as Strings
questions.body:
Given two non-negative integers num1 and num2 represented as strings, return the product of num1 and num2, also represented as a string. You must not use any built-in BigInteger library or convert the inputs to integer directly.

Example 1
Input: num1 = "2", num2 = "3"
Output: "6"
Example 2
Input: num1 = "123", num2 = "456"
Output: "56088"

Constraints

  • 1 <= num1.length, num2.length <= 200
  • num1 and num2 consist of digits only.
  • Both do not contain leading zeros, except the number 0 itself.
questions.answer:
Problem: Multiply two non-negative integers given as strings (may not fit in 64-bit).

Idea — grade-school multiplication:

  1. Result array of size n+m. For digits num1[i], num2[j], add product into pos[i+j+1], carry into pos[i+j].
  2. Walk the array converting digits to a string; skip leading zeros.

Complexity: O(n·m) time, O(n+m) space. Edge: either operand "0"; leading zeros in input (normalise).

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Find All Pairs with Given Sum in Two Arrays
questions.body:
Given two integer arrays A and B and an integer K, print all pairs (a, b) such that a is from A, b is from B, and a + b = K. If a value appears multiple times, each occurrence can form a pair (do not drop duplicates).

Example 1
Input: A = [1, 2, 4, 5, 7], B = [5, 6, 3, 4, 8], K = 9
Output: (1, 8), (2, 7), (4, 5), (5, 4)
Explanation: Order of pairs does not matter.
Example 2
Input: A = [1, 1, 2], B = [3, 4], K = 5
Output: (1, 4), (1, 4), (2, 3)
Explanation: Both 1's in A pair with 4.

Constraints

  • 1 <= A.length, B.length <= 10^5
  • -10^9 <= values, K <= 10^9
questions.answer:
Problem: All pairs (a from A, b from B) with a+b = K.

Idea: Put all of A into a multiset/map (or set if uniqueness allowed). For each b in B, check if K-b exists in A.

If duplicates matter: use frequency maps, not a plain set — a set drops duplicate keys and under-counts pairs.

Complexity: O(N+M) expected with hashing. Follow-up: sorted arrays → two pointers without extra space.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Increasing Triplet Subsequence
questions.body:
Given an integer array nums, return true if there exists a triple of indices (i, j, k) such that i < j < k and nums[i] < nums[j] < nums[k]. Otherwise return false.

Example 1
Input: nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
Output: true
Explanation: Any increasing triple works, e.g. (0, 1, 2).
Example 2
Input: nums = [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]
Output: false
Explanation: No increasing triple of indices exists.

Constraints

  • 1 <= nums.length <= 5 * 10^5
  • -2^31 <= nums[i] <= 2^31 - 1
questions.answer:
Problem: Exists indices i < j < k with a[i] < a[j] < a[k]?

Idea — one pass, track two minima:

  1. first = smallest so far; second = smallest number that already has a smaller to its left.
  2. On seeing x: if x <= first update first; else if x <= second update second; else you found a third → true.

Complexity: O(N) time, O(1) space. Beat the O(N²) DP. Trap: equalities — use strict < as stated.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Maximum j–i such that arr[j] > arr[i]
questions.body:
Given an array arr[], find the maximum value of j - i such that arr[j] > arr[i] and j > i. If no such pair exists, return -1.

Example 1
Input: arr = [34, 8, 10, 3, 2, 80, 30, 33, 1]
Output: 6
Explanation: arr[1] = 8 and arr[7] = 33, and 7 - 1 = 6 is maximum.
Example 2
Input: arr = [9, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 18, 0]
Output: 8
Explanation: arr[0] = 9 and arr[8] = 18.

Constraints

  • 1 <= n <= 10^5
  • 1 <= arr[i] <= 10^9
questions.answer:
Problem: Maximise j−i subject to arr[j] > arr[i] (or ≥ depending on statement — confirm with interviewer).

Idea — left-min / right-max + two pointers:

  1. Lmin[i] = min on [0..i]; Rmax[j] = max on [j..n-1].
  2. Two pointers from left/right: if Lmin[i] < Rmax[j] (or ≤), update answer and try larger span by moving j; else move i.

Complexity: O(N). Clarify strict vs non-strict comparison — GFG “Maximum Index” often uses ≤.

solutions.label: C++

questions.hint: Pre-compute leftMin[] and rightMax[], then use two-pointer to find max (j-i).

questions.title: Maximize Sum Picking K Elements from Either Side
questions.body:
There are several cards arranged in a row, and each card has an associated number of points. The points are given in the integer array cardPoints. In one step, you can take one card from the beginning or from the end of the row. You have to take exactly k cards. Return the maximum number of points you can obtain.

Example 1
Input: cardPoints = [1,2,3,4,5,6,1], k = 3
Output: 12
Explanation: Take the three cards on the right: 1 + 6 + 5 = 12.
Example 2
Input: cardPoints = [9,7,7,9,7,7,9], k = 7
Output: 55
Explanation: You have to take all the cards.

Constraints

  • 1 <= cardPoints.length <= 10^5
  • 1 <= cardPoints[i] <= 10^4
  • 1 <= k <= cardPoints.length
questions.answer:
Problem: Pick exactly K elements from either end of the array; maximise their sum.

Equivalence: leaving a contiguous middle of length n−K. Minimising that middle sum maximises the ends’ sum.

  1. Compute total sum; find minimum sum subarray of length n−K (sliding window); answer = total − that min.
  2. Or explicitly try taking i from left and K−i from right using prefix/suffix sums.

Complexity: O(N). Edge: K=n (take all); K=0.

solutions.label: C++

questions.hint: Equivalent to minimising the sum of a middle window of length n−K (complement of picks from both ends). Or expand prefix/suffix sums of length K.

questions.title: Sort Array by Frequency of Elements
questions.body:
Given an integer array nums, sort it by decreasing frequency of values. If two values have the same frequency, the smaller value comes first.

Example 1
Input: nums = [2, 3, 1, 3, 2]
Output: [2, 2, 3, 3, 1]
Explanation: 2 and 3 both appear twice; 2 is smaller, so it comes first. 1 appears once.
Example 2
Input: nums = [1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3]
Output: [2, 2, 2, 1, 1, 3]

Constraints

  • 1 <= nums.length <= 10^5
  • -10^4 <= nums[i] <= 10^4
questions.answer:
Problem: Sort by frequency (higher first); ties by value (define order with interviewer).

Idea: count frequencies → sort unique keys with comparator (freq desc, value asc/desc) → expand back to array.

Complexity: O(N log U) for U unique keys. Alt: bucket sort by frequency for O(N + maxFreq) if values bounded.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Find First and Last Position in Sorted Array (Binary Search)
questions.body:
Given an array of integers nums sorted in non-decreasing order, find the starting and ending position of a given target. If target is not found, return [-1, -1]. You must write an algorithm with O(log n) runtime.

Example 1
Input: nums = [5,7,7,8,8,10], target = 8
Output: [3, 4]
Example 2
Input: nums = [5,7,7,8,8,10], target = 6
Output: [-1, -1]

Constraints

  • 0 <= nums.length <= 10^5
  • -10^9 <= nums[i], target <= 10^9
  • nums is sorted non-decreasing.
questions.answer:
Problem: First and last index of target in a sorted array (with duplicates).

Idea — two binary searches:

  1. Lower bound: first index ≥ target (or == target).
  2. Upper bound: first index > target, then last = that − 1.

If lower bound misses target, return [-1,-1].

Complexity: O(log N). Do not scan linearly after finding one hit — that’s O(N) worst case on all duplicates.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Reverse Linked List in Groups of K
questions.body:
Given the head of a linked list, reverse the nodes of the list k at a time, and return the modified list. k is a positive integer and is less than or equal to the length of the linked list. If the number of nodes is not a multiple of k, the leftover nodes at the end stay in their original order.

Example 1
Input: head = [1,2,3,4,5], k = 2
Output: [2,1,4,3,5]
Example 2
Input: head = [1,2,3,4,5], k = 3
Output: [3,2,1,4,5]

Constraints

  • The number of nodes is in [1, 5000].
  • 0 <= Node.val <= 1000
  • 1 <= k <= number of nodes
questions.answer:
Problem: Reverse nodes in groups of K; leftover < K stay as-is (usual LC #25 rule — confirm).

Idea:

  1. Count K nodes ahead; if fewer than K, stop.
  2. Reverse that segment in-place; connect previous group’s tail to new head; recurse/iterate on rest.

Complexity: O(N) time, O(1) extra (iterative) or O(N/K) recursion depth. Draw pointers on paper before coding.

solutions.label: C++

questions.source: Reported: MMT Set-4 GFG, SSE-2 Nov 2023

questions.title: Clone Linked List with Next and Random Pointers
questions.body:
A linked list of length n is given such that each node contains an additional random pointer, which could point to any node in the list, or null. Construct a deep copy of the list. The deep copy should consist of exactly n brand new nodes, and none of the pointers in the new list should point to nodes in the original list. Return the head of the copied list.

Example 1
Input: head = [[7,null],[13,0],[11,4],[10,2],[1,0]]
Output: [[7,null],[13,0],[11,4],[10,2],[1,0]]
Explanation: Each pair is [val, random_index]. The copy has the same structure but new nodes.
Example 2
Input: head = [[1,1],[2,1]]
Output: [[1,1],[2,1]]
Explanation: Node 1's random points to itself; node 2's random points to node 1.

Constraints

  • 0 <= n <= 1000
  • -10^4 <= Node.val <= 10^4
  • random is null or points to a node in the list.
questions.answer:
Problem: Deep-copy list where each node has next and random.

O(1) space weave method:

  1. Interleave copy nodes: A → A' → B → B'.
  2. Set A'.random = A.random.next (the copy sitting after original random).
  3. Unweave into original and clone lists.

Alt: HashMap old→new then second pass for random — O(N) space, simpler.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Populate Next Right Pointers in Each Node
questions.body:
You are given a perfect binary tree where all leaves are on the same level, and every parent has two children. Populate each next pointer to point to its next right node. If there is no next right node, next should be null. Initially every next is null. Return the root.

Example 1
Input: root = [1,2,3,4,5,6,7]
Output: [1,#,2,3,#,4,5,6,7,#]
Explanation: '#' marks the end of a level. 2.next = 3, 4.next = 5, 5.next = 6, 6.next = 7.
Example 2
Input: root = []
Output: []

Constraints

  • The number of nodes is in [0, 2^12 - 1].
  • The tree is a perfect binary tree.
questions.answer:
Problem: Populate next pointers to the right sibling (perfect binary tree LC #116).

O(1) space: level by level using already-set next. For node with left/right: left.next = right; right.next = parent.next.left if parent.next exists.

Clarify: LC #117 (any tree) needs a different BFS/queue or carefully threaded approach. Comment space carefully — perfect-tree O(1) vs queue O(width).

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Intersection of Two Linked Lists (Merge Point)
questions.body:
Given the heads of two singly linked lists headA and headB, return the node at which the two lists intersect. If the two linked lists have no intersection, return null. The lists share structure after the intersection (not just equal values).

Example 1
Input: listA = [4,1,8,4,5], listB = [5,6,1,8,4,5], skipA = 2, skipB = 3
Output: Intersected at node with value 8
Explanation: The shared tail starts at the node 8.
Example 2
Input: listA = [2,6,4], listB = [1,5]
Output: null
Explanation: The lists do not intersect.

Constraints

  • The number of nodes of listA is m.
  • The number of nodes of listB is n.
  • 1 <= m, n <= 3 * 10^4
questions.answer:
Problem: Find merge point of two singly linked lists (Y-shape).

Two-pointer switch: pointers traverse A then B (and vice versa). When lengths differ, after switch they align and meet at intersection (or both null).

Complexity: O(N+M) time, O(1) space. Alt: length diff method; HashSet of nodes.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Reverse Second Half of Linked List (In-Place)
questions.body:
Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse only the second half in-place and return the head. For an odd-length list, the first half is the longer one (the middle node stays in the first half). Do this in O(1) extra space.

Example 1
Input: head = [1,2,3,4,5]
Output: [1,2,3,5,4]
Explanation: Second half is [4,5], reversed to [5,4].
Example 2
Input: head = [1,2,3,4]
Output: [1,2,4,3]
Explanation: Second half is [3,4], reversed to [4,3].

Constraints

  • 0 <= number of nodes <= 10^4
  • 0 <= Node.val <= 1000
questions.answer:
Problem: Reverse only the second half of the list in-place.

Steps:

  1. Guard empty / single node.
  2. Slow/fast to find mid (slow at end of first half).
  3. Standard iterative reverse from slow→next; reconnect slow→next = newHead.

Complexity: O(N) / O(1). Decide odd-length mid convention with interviewer (first half longer vs second).

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: LCA / Common Manager of Two Employees
questions.body:
You are given an org chart: each employee has a name and a parent (manager) pointer, forming a tree rooted at the CEO. Given two employees a and b, return their closest common manager (the lowest common ancestor). You may design the Employee class.

Example 1
Input: CEO
       /  \
      A    C
     /
    B
a = B, b = C
Output: CEO
Explanation: CEO is the closest manager shared by B and C.
Example 2
Input: same tree, a = A, b = B
Output: A
Explanation: A manages B, so A is the closest common manager.

Constraints

  • The org chart is a tree (one parent each, except CEO).
  • a and b exist in the tree.
questions.answer:
Problem: LCA framed as “common manager” of two employees.

With parent pointers: walk both to root collecting ancestors; first shared is LCA. Or depth-align then climb together.

Classic BT LCA (no parent): recurse — if root is p or q return root; if both sides nonempty return root; else return nonempty side.

Complexity: O(N). Mention MMT often uses the org-chart / parent-pointer story.

solutions.label: C++

questions.source: Reported: SDE/SSE-2 LeetCode Oct 2024, Code360 Oct 2022
questions.hint: Disguised as "common manager" — it's LCA on a general tree. Key insight: if the Emp class has a parent pointer, walk both nodes to root, collect ancestors, find first match.

questions.title: Validate Binary Search Tree
questions.body:
Given the root of a binary tree, determine if it is a valid binary search tree (BST). A valid BST is defined as follows: the left subtree of a node contains only nodes with keys less than the node's key; the right subtree contains only nodes with keys greater than the node's key; both subtrees are also BSTs.

Example 1
Input: root = [2,1,3]
Output: true
Example 2
Input: root = [5,1,4,null,null,3,6]
Output: false
Explanation: 3 is in the right subtree of 5 but is not greater than 5.

Constraints

  • The number of nodes is in [1, 10^4].
  • -2^31 <= Node.val <= 2^31 - 1
questions.answer:
Problem: Validate BST — every node in (low, high) range.

Idea: DFS with bounds. Left child must be < node.val with updated high; right > node with updated low. Use long sentinels to avoid INT overflow.

Wrong approach: only check local parent-child — misses deeper violations.

Complexity: O(N). Inorder strictly increasing is an equivalent check.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Left View of Binary Tree
questions.body:
Given the root of a binary tree, return the left view: the list of node values you see if you stand on the left side of the tree (the first node of each level from the left).

Example 1
Input: root = [1,2,3,4,5]
Output: [1,2,4]
Explanation: Level 0 shows 1, level 1 shows 2 (before 3), level 2 shows 4 (before 5).
Example 2
Input: root = [1,2,3,null,4,null,null,5]
Output: [1,2,4,5]

Constraints

  • The number of nodes is in [0, 10^4].
  • -100 <= Node.val <= 100
questions.answer:
Problem: Left view — first node seen at each depth from the left.

DFS: preorder preferring left; record node when depth first visited.

BFS: level-order; take the first node of each level.

Complexity: O(N). Symmetric for right view (prefer right / take last in level).

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Vertical Order Traversal of Binary Tree
questions.body:
Given the root of a binary tree, return its vertical order traversal. Columns are indexed by horizontal distance (root = 0, left child = parent − 1, right child = parent + 1). Within a column, nodes appear top to bottom. Return columns from leftmost to rightmost.

Example 1
Input: root = [3,9,20,null,null,15,7]
Output: [[9],[3,15],[20],[7]]
Example 2
Input: root = [1,2,3,4,5,6,7]
Output: [[4],[2],[1,5,6],[3],[7]]

Constraints

  • The number of nodes is in [0, 1000].
  • -1000 <= Node.val <= 1000
questions.answer:
Problem: Vertical order — group nodes by horizontal distance (root 0, left −1, right +1).

BFS + map: queue of (node, hd); insert into map<hd, list>. BFS keeps top-to-bottom order within a column. Sort keys for left→right output.

LC 987 also sorts by row then value — clarify which variant.

Complexity: O(N log C) if tree-map, C = distinct columns.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Path Finding in Binary Matrix (Backtracking / Rat in Maze)
questions.body:
You are given an n x m binary matrix grid. A cell with 0 is open; a cell with 1 is a wall. You start at (0, 0) and want to reach (n-1, m-1). You may move up, down, left, or right through open cells. Return true if any path exists, otherwise false. Assume the start and end cells are open.

Example 1
Input: grid = [[0,0,1],[0,0,0],[1,0,0]]
Output: true
Explanation: One path is (0,0) → (1,0) → (1,1) → (1,2) → (2,2).
Example 2
Input: grid = [[0,1],[1,0]]
Output: false
Explanation: The destination is blocked off from the start.

Constraints

  • 1 <= n, m <= 100
  • grid[i][j] is 0 or 1.
questions.answer:
Problem: Path in binary matrix / rat-in-maze — move to destination on open cells.

Backtracking / DFS: mark visited, try 4 (or 8) directions, unmark on failure (if paths must reuse). BFS if only existence/shortest path needed.

Complexity: exponential worst-case for all paths; BFS shortest is O(N²) on grid.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Cut Tree to Minimise Subtree Sum Difference
questions.body:
A tree has n nodes (0-indexed) and n-1 edges. Each node has an integer value. Choose one edge to remove so that the absolute difference between the sums of the two resulting components is minimised. Return that minimum difference.

Example 1
Input: n = 4, edges = [[0,1],[0,2],[0,3]], values = [6,2,4,1]
Output: 5
Explanation: Cutting 0-2 splits sums 4 and 9; |4-9| = 5, which is the minimum.
Example 2
Input: n = 2, edges = [[0,1]], values = [1,1]
Output: 0

Constraints

  • 2 <= n <= 10^5
  • The graph is a tree.
  • -10^4 <= values[i] <= 10^4
questions.answer:
Problem: Remove one edge to minimise |sum(component1) − sum(component2)|.

Idea: total sum S. DFS returns subtree sum sub. Cutting the edge to parent splits into sub and S−sub; difference |S−2·sub|.

Critical: do not update the answer at the root (no edge above root) — that forces difference 0 incorrectly.

Complexity: O(N).

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Critical Connections in Network (Bridges — Tarjan's)
questions.body:
There are n servers numbered from 0 to n - 1 connected by undirected connections. A critical connection is an edge whose removal disconnects the network. Return all critical connections (bridges). You may return the answer in any order.

Example 1
Input: n = 4, connections = [[0,1],[1,2],[2,0],[1,3]]
Output: [[1,3]]
Explanation: Removing [1,3] disconnects server 3. The triangle 0-1-2 has no bridge.
Example 2
Input: n = 2, connections = [[0,1]]
Output: [[0,1]]

Constraints

  • 2 <= n <= 10^5
  • 1 <= connections.length <= 10^5
  • 0 <= ai, bi <= n - 1
  • No repeated edges; the graph may be disconnected.
questions.answer:
Problem: Critical connections / bridges in an undirected graph.

Tarjan: discovery time tin, low-link low. Edge u–v is a bridge if low[v] > tin[u] (subtree of v can’t reach u or above).

Complexity: O(V+E). Handle multi-edges carefully; ignore parent edge in undirected DFS.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Shortest Path in Graph (Dijkstra)
questions.body:
You are given a weighted undirected graph with n nodes and a source node src. Edge weights are non-negative. Return an array dist where dist[i] is the shortest-path distance from src to i. If a node is unreachable, use -1.

Example 1
Input: n = 5, edges = [[0,1,2],[0,2,4],[1,2,1],[1,3,7],[2,4,3]], src = 0
Output: [0, 2, 3, 9, 6]
Explanation: 0→1 is 2; 0→1→2 is 3; 0→1→3 is 9; 0→1→2→4 is 6.
Example 2
Input: n = 3, edges = [[0,1,1]], src = 0
Output: [0, 1, -1]

Constraints

  • 1 <= n <= 10^4
  • 0 <= edges.length <= 10^5
  • 0 <= weight <= 10^4
questions.answer:
Problem: Shortest paths from a source on non-negative weighted graph.

Dijkstra: min-heap of (dist, node); relax neighbours when improvement found. Skip outdated heap entries.

Complexity: O((V+E) log V) binary heap. Not for negative weights — use Bellman-Ford. Unweighted → plain BFS.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Coordinate Reachability Check Using GCD
questions.body:
You start at coordinate (1, 1). In one move from (a, b) you may go to (a+b, b) or (a, a+b). Given positive integers x and y, return true if (x, y) is reachable, otherwise false.

Example 1
Input: x = 3, y = 5
Output: true
Explanation: gcd(3, 5) = 1, and every move preserves gcd, starting from gcd(1, 1) = 1.
Example 2
Input: x = 2, y = 4
Output: false
Explanation: gcd(2, 4) = 2 ≠ 1, so (2, 4) is unreachable.

Constraints

  • 1 <= x, y <= 10^9
questions.answer:
Problem: From (1,1) moves (a,b)→(a+b,b) or (a,a+b); can you reach (x,y)?

Insight: moves preserve gcd. Since gcd(1,1)=1, reachable iff gcd(x,y)==1 (for positive targets as stated).

Complexity: O(log min(x,y)). Confirm constraints (only positive quadrant, etc.).

solutions.label: C++

questions.hint: From (1,1) move to (a+b,b) or (a,a+b). Reach (x,y)? Key: gcd(x,y) must equal 1 since gcd is preserved by moves and gcd(1,1)=1.

questions.title: Maximum Sum Increasing Subsequence
questions.body:
Given an array of n positive integers, find the maximum sum of an increasing subsequence (elements need not be contiguous, but must stay in order and be strictly increasing).

Example 1
Input: arr = [1, 101, 2, 3, 100, 4, 5]
Output: 106
Explanation: 1 + 2 + 3 + 100 = 106.
Example 2
Input: arr = [10, 5, 4, 3]
Output: 10
Explanation: The best increasing subsequence is just [10].

Constraints

  • 1 <= n <= 1000
  • 1 <= arr[i] <= 10^5
questions.answer:
Problem: Maximum sum of an increasing subsequence (not necessarily contiguous).

DP: dp[i] = val[i] + max{ dp[j] | j<i, val[j]<val[i] } (or just val[i]). Answer = max dp.

Complexity: O(N²). Mentions of O(N log N) usually refer to length (Patience LIS), not sum — different problem.

solutions.label: C++

questions.hint: dp[i] = max sum increasing subsequence ending at i. O(N²) naive, O(N log N) with BIT.

questions.title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
questions.body:
Given an unsorted array of integers nums, return the length of the longest consecutive elements sequence. You must write an algorithm that runs in O(n) time.

Example 1
Input: nums = [100,4,200,1,3,2]
Output: 4
Explanation: The longest consecutive sequence is [1, 2, 3, 4].
Example 2
Input: nums = [0,3,7,2,5,8,4,6,0,1]
Output: 9
Explanation: The sequence is 0 through 8.

Constraints

  • 0 <= nums.length <= 10^5
  • -10^9 <= nums[i] <= 10^9
questions.answer:
Problem: Longest consecutive sequence in unsorted array — O(N) expected.

HashSet: insert all. Only start a streak at x when x−1 absent; count x, x+1, ….

Each number enters the inner loop once → O(N). Sorting would be O(N log N).

solutions.label: C++

questions.hint: Put all nums in a HashSet. Only start a streak from x when x−1 is absent; walk x, x+1, … O(N).

questions.title: Generate All Permutations of a String
questions.body:
Given a string s of distinct characters, return all permutations of s. You may return them in any order. Follow-up: if s contains duplicate characters, return each unique permutation once.

Example 1
Input: s = "ABC"
Output: ["ABC","ACB","BAC","BCA","CAB","CBA"]
Example 2
Input: s = "AAB"
Output: ["AAB","ABA","BAA"]
Explanation: Duplicate-aware follow-up — each distinct permutation once.

Constraints

  • 1 <= s.length <= 8
  • s consists of English letters.
questions.answer:
Problem: All permutations of a string / array.

Backtracking: swap-choose-recurse-unswap, or build path with used[]. Deduplicate with sort + skip identical siblings if duplicates exist.

Complexity: O(N·N!) time to output. Discuss heap’s algorithm only if asked.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Dice Throw — Count ways to achieve target sum
questions.body:
Given n dice, each with f faces numbered 1 to f, return the number of ways to get sum target. Since the answer may be large, return it modulo 10^9 + 7. Two ways are different if at least one die shows a different face.

Example 1
Input: n = 1, f = 6, target = 3
Output: 1
Explanation: Only (3).
Example 2
Input: n = 2, f = 6, target = 7
Output: 6
Explanation: (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1).

Constraints

  • 1 <= n, f <= 30
  • 1 <= target <= 1000
questions.answer:
Problem: Number of ways to get sum X with N dice of F faces.

DP: dp[n][s] = ways with n dice summing to s. Transition: add face 1..F from dp[n−1][s−face].

Space-optimise to 1D rolling arrays. Mod 10^9+7 if required.

Complexity: O(N·X·F).

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Generate N Pairs of Balanced Parentheses
questions.body:
Given n pairs of parentheses, write a function to generate all combinations of well-formed parentheses.

Example 1
Input: n = 2
Output: ["(())","()()"]
Example 2
Input: n = 3
Output: ["((()))","(()())","(())()","()(())","()()()"]

Constraints

  • 1 <= n <= 8
questions.answer:
Problem: All strings with N pairs of balanced parentheses.

Backtracking: place ( while open < N; place ) while close < open. Catalan number of results.

Complexity: O(C_n · n) output-sensitive. Classic recursion tree dry-run favourite.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Longest Repeating Non-Overlapping Substring
questions.body:
Given a string s, find the longest substring that appears at least twice in s without overlapping. If several answers have the same length, return any. If none exists, return "".

Example 1
Input: s = "aab"
Output: "a"
Explanation: "a" occurs at indices 0 and 1 and those occurrences do not overlap.
Example 2
Input: s = "aabaabaaba"
Output: "aaba"
Explanation: "aaba" starts at index 0 and again at index 4; the spans [0,3] and [4,7] do not overlap.

Constraints

  • 1 <= s.length <= 500
  • s consists of lowercase English letters.
questions.answer:
Problem: Longest repeating non-overlapping substring (classic DP variant).

DP: dp[i][j] = length of repeating substring ending at i and j with no overlap (|i−j| > dp). Track global max length/substring.

Complexity: O(N²). Clarify exact GFG statement — definitions vary slightly.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Maximum Frequency Stack (FreqStack)
questions.body:
Design a stack-like data structure FreqStack that supports push(int val) and pop(). pop removes and returns the most frequent element. If there is a tie, remove the one closest to the top of the stack.

Example 1
Input:
["FreqStack","push","push","push","push","push","push","pop","pop","pop","pop"]
[[],[5],[7],[5],[7],[4],[5],[],[],[],[]]
Output: [null,null,null,null,null,null,null,5,7,5,4]
Explanation: 5 is most frequent (3). After popping it, 5 and 7 both have frequency 2; 7 was pushed later, so pop 7 next.
Example 2
Input: push(1), push(1), pop(), pop()
Output: 1, 1

Constraints

  • At most 2 * 10^4 calls.
  • 0 <= val <= 10^9
  • pop is never called on an empty stack.
questions.answer:
Problem: FreqStack — push/pop; pop most frequent, ties → most recent.

Structure: val→freq map; freq→stack of vals; track maxfreq. Push updates freq and pushes into that freq’s stack. Pop from maxfreq stack; decrease freq; maybe decrement maxfreq.

Complexity: Amortised O(1) per op. Beautiful MMT/heap alternative discussion.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Kth Largest Element
questions.body:
Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the kth largest element in the array. Note that it is the kth largest in sorted order, not the kth distinct element.

Example 1
Input: nums = [3,2,1,5,6,4], k = 2
Output: 5
Example 2
Input: nums = [3,2,3,1,2,4,5,5,6], k = 4
Output: 4

Constraints

  • 1 <= k <= nums.length <= 10^5
  • -10^4 <= nums[i] <= 10^4
questions.answer:
Problem: Kth largest in array (or stream).

Heap-of-K: min-heap size K; push if larger than top; top is Kth largest.

Complexity: O(N log K). Quickselect expected O(N). Stream variant: same heap maintained online.

solutions.label: C++

questions.source: Reported: SDE-2 Code360 May 2022, MMT Set-4

questions.title: LRU Cache
questions.body:
Design a data structure that follows the constraints of a Least Recently Used (LRU) cache. Implement LRUCache(int capacity), get(int key) (return the value, or -1 if missing; counts as a use), and put(int key, int value) (insert or update; if over capacity, evict the least recently used key). Both operations must be O(1) average time.

Example 1
Input:
["LRUCache","put","put","get","put","get","put","get","get","get"]
[[2],[1,1],[2,2],[1],[3,3],[2],[4,4],[1],[3],[4]]
Output: [null,null,null,1,null,-1,null,-1,3,4]
Explanation: capacity 2. put(3,3) evicts key 2. put(4,4) evicts key 1.
Example 2
Input: capacity = 1; put(1,1); put(2,2); get(1); get(2)
Output: -1, 2

Constraints

  • 1 <= capacity <= 3000
  • 0 <= key, value <= 10^4
  • At most 2 * 10^5 calls.
questions.answer:
Problem: LRU Cache — O(1) get/put.

HashMap + doubly linked list: map key→node; list order = recency (head newest). get moves node to head; put updates/evicts tail when over capacity.

Complexity: O(1) average. Mention Java LinkedHashMap access-order as production shortcut, but implement DLL in interviews.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Stack Using Queue / Queue Using Stack
questions.body:
Implement a stack using queues, and a queue using stacks. Support the usual operations: for the stack, push, pop, top, empty; for the queue, push, pop, peek, empty. State the complexity of each operation.

Example 1
Stack using queues:
push(1)
push(2)
top()
Output: 2
pop()
Output: 2
empty()
Output: false
Example 2
Queue using two stacks:
push(1)
push(2)
peek()
Output: 1
pop()
Output: 1
pop()
Output: 2
empty()
Output: true

Constraints

  • 1 <= x <= 9
  • At most 100 calls.
  • pop/top/peek are never called on an empty structure.
questions.answer:
Problem: Implement stack using queues and/or queue using stacks.

Stack via queue: on push, enqueue then rotate older elements behind (or lazy on pop).

Queue via two stacks: in-stack for enqueue; out-stack for dequeue — pour when out empty (amortised O(1)).

State which variant you implement and complexity of each op.

solutions.label: C++

categories.title: Concurrency Coding (C++ reference; implement in Java at MMT)

questions.title: Implement HashMap from Scratch — Thread-Safe
questions.category: Concurrency Coding (C++ reference; implement in Java at MMT)
questions.body:
Implement a hash map from scratch in Java with put(key, value), get(key), and remove(key). Handle collisions with separate chaining. Then make put thread-safe. Be ready to explain why the default capacity is 16 and why capacity stays a power of two.

Example 1
Input: put(1, 10), put(2, 20), get(1), put(2, 30), get(2), remove(1), get(1)
Output: 10, 30, null
Explanation: The second put updates key 2. After remove, key 1 is absent.
Example 2
Input: two threads call put on different keys at the same time
Output: both entries are visible afterwards; neither write is lost.
Explanation: A global synchronized put is correct but coarse. Per-bucket / striped locking is the expected discussion.

Constraints

  • Keys and values are integers for the coding part.
  • Load factor 0.75; rehash when size exceeds capacity * load factor.
questions.answer:
Problem: Thread-safe HashMap from scratch (MMT loves Java follow-up).

Core: array of buckets; hash & (cap−1) requires power-of-two capacity; separate chaining; rehash at load factor 0.75.

Thread-safety: synchronize per bucket / striped locks (ConcurrentHashMap inspiration), or ConcurrentHashMap segments. Naive global synchronized is correct but contended.

Explain why capacity 16 and bitmask vs modulo — classic MMT Q.

solutions.label: C++

questions.source: Reported: Senior SDE GFG 2019, Glassdoor Java Developer
questions.hint: MMT interviewers want you to implement this in Java with thread-safe put(). Follow-up: why default capacity is 16 (power-of-2 allows bitmask: hash & (n-1) instead of modulo).

questions.title: Multi-threaded HTML Word Counter
questions.category: Concurrency Coding (C++ reference; implement in Java at MMT)
questions.body:
You are given a list of URLs and a keyword. Download the HTML of each URL concurrently and count how many times the keyword occurs in each page. Return a list of [url, keyword, count]. A failed download should not fail the whole batch — record count -1 for that URL.

Example 1
Input: urls = ["https://a.example", "https://b.example"], keyword = "offer"
Page a contains "offer" twice; page b contains it zero times.
Output: [["https://a.example","offer",2], ["https://b.example","offer",0]]
Example 2
Input: urls = ["https://down.example"], keyword = "mmt"
The download throws / times out.
Output: [["https://down.example","mmt",-1]]

Constraints

  • 1 <= urls.length <= 100
  • Use a thread pool or CompletableFuture, not one thread per URL unbounded.
  • Do not block the common ForkJoinPool on network I/O.
questions.answer:
Problem: Download several HTML pages concurrently; count occurrences of a keyword; gather results.

Java approach: ExecutorService / CompletableFuture per URL; each task returns (url, keyword, count); AtomicInteger only if sharing one counter. Join with invokeAll / allOf.

Discuss timeouts, failure isolation, and not blocking the common ForkJoin pool on I/O — use a dedicated executor.

solutions.label: C++

questions.source: Reported: Tech Lead LeetCode Discuss Jul 2024
questions.hint: Download pages concurrently, count string occurrences. Must use Java threading (CompletableFuture / ExecutorService). Output: [url, keyword, count].

questions.title: Thread-Safe Builder Pattern (AtomicReference approach)
questions.category: Concurrency Coding (C++ reference; implement in Java at MMT)
questions.body:
Implement a thread-safe Builder that several threads may use to set fields of an object and then build() it. The interviewer will reject a solution that synchronizes every setter as “blocking”. Prefer an immutable builder (each setter returns a new builder) or AtomicReference / CAS.

Example 1
Input: thread A sets name = "Ash", thread B sets role = "SDE"; then build()
Output: a single object {name: "Ash", role: "SDE"} with no torn fields.
Explanation: Immutable copies (or a CAS loop on the product) publish a consistent snapshot.
Example 2
Input: two threads set the same field, last write wins
Output: exactly one of the two values is visible; never a partial string / half-updated reference.

Constraints

  • Fields are references or immutables.
  • build() must be safe to call once the setters that should be included have happened.
questions.answer:
Problem: Thread-safe Builder — interviewers may reject coarse synchronized.

Options:

  • Immutable builder: each setter returns a new builder copy — no shared mutable state.
  • AtomicReference<T>: CAS the product being built.

Explain why synchronized works but is “blocking”; show you know non-blocking alternatives.

solutions.label: C++

questions.hint: MMT interviewer rejected synchronized as "blocking". Expected Atomic-based or immutable builder solution.

questions.title: Tower of Hanoi
questions.body:
The Tower of Hanoi puzzle has three rods and n disks of different sizes, stacked on the source rod in decreasing size. Move the entire stack to the target rod, using the auxiliary rod. You may move only one disk at a time, and you may never place a larger disk on a smaller one. Print the sequence of moves, or return the number of moves.

Example 1
Input: n = 2, from = "A", to = "C", aux = "B"
Output:
Move disk 1 from A to B
Move disk 2 from A to C
Move disk 1 from B to C
Explanation: 3 moves = 2^2 - 1.
Example 2
Input: n = 3
Output: 7 moves
Explanation: T(n) = 2T(n-1) + 1 = 2^n - 1.

Constraints

  • 1 <= n <= 16 if you print every move.
  • Rod names are distinct.
questions.answer:
Problem: Tower of Hanoi — move N disks from src to dest via aux.

Recurrence: move N−1 to aux, move largest to dest, move N−1 onto dest. T(N)=2T(N−1)+1 = 2^N−1 moves.

Dry-run N=3; mention stack depth O(N).

solutions.label: C++

questions.hint: Classic recursion: move n−1 to aux, move largest to target, move n−1 onto target. T(n)=2T(n−1)+1.

questions.title: Shortest Unsorted Subarray
questions.body:
Given an integer array nums, you need to find the shortest contiguous subarray that, if sorted, makes the whole array sorted in non-decreasing order. Return the length of that subarray. If the array is already sorted, return 0.

Example 1
Input: nums = [2,6,4,8,10,9,15]
Output: 5
Explanation: Sort [6,4,8,10,9] and the whole array becomes sorted.
Example 2
Input: nums = [1,2,3,4]
Output: 0

Constraints

  • 1 <= nums.length <= 10^4
  • -10^5 <= nums[i] <= 10^5
questions.answer:
Problem: Shortest unsorted continuous subarray that, if sorted, sorts the whole array.

Idea: find leftmost index not matching sorted order / or one-pass: track max from left and min from right to find the window boundaries.

Complexity: O(N) clever pass or O(N log N) via sorting copy. Edge: already sorted → length 0.

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Josephus Problem — Circular array, remove Kth, find last
questions.body:
There are n people standing in a circle, numbered 1 to n. Counting begins at 1 and proceeds around the circle. Every k-th person is eliminated until only one remains. Return the number of the last remaining person (1-indexed).

Example 1
Input: n = 5, k = 2
Output: 3
Explanation: Eliminate 2, 4, 1, 5 in that order. 3 remains.
Example 2
Input: n = 7, k = 3
Output: 4

Constraints

  • 1 <= k <= n <= 10^5
questions.answer:
Problem: Josephus — every K-th person eliminated in a circle; find survivor.

DP: f(1)=0 (0-based); f(n)=(f(n−1)+K) % n; convert to 1-based if needed.

Complexity: O(N). Simulation with queue is O(NK).

solutions.label: C++

questions.title: Prisoner Wall Jump Problem
questions.body:
A prisoner must cross n walls. Wall i has height h[i]. In one jump the prisoner gains H units of height. If the wall is not yet cleared, they slip down L units before the next jump. After a wall is cleared, height resets to 0 for the next wall. Return the total number of jumps needed to clear every wall. If it is impossible (no net progress, and a wall is taller than H), return -1.

Example 1
Input: h = [10, 10], H = 5, L = 1
Output: 6
Explanation: For one wall of 10: jump to 5 (slip to 4), jump to 9 (slip to 8), jump to 13 (cleared). 3 jumps × 2 walls = 6.
Example 2
Input: h = [10], H = 5, L = 5
Output: -1
Explanation: After a failed jump, height returns to 0, so a wall taller than H can never be cleared.

Constraints

  • 1 <= n <= 10^4
  • 1 <= h[i], H <= 10^5
  • 0 <= L <= 10^5
questions.answer:
Problem: Prisoner jumps walls of heights h[i] with jump H and slip L each failed attempt.

Per wall: accumulate height += H each jump; if still below wall, slip −L and continue. Count jumps.

Critical: if H ≤ L, net progress after a failed jump is ≤0 → infinite loop on tall walls. Return −1 (impossible) unless h[i] ≤ H (cleared in one jump).

solutions.label: C++

questions.hint: For each wall, keep jumping +H and slipping −L until height clears the wall. If H ≤ L, only walls with height ≤ H are possible (one jump); taller walls are impossible.

questions.title: Store Open/Close Timing — Availability Check (Implementation)
questions.body:
A store has several open intervals. open[i] and close[i] are the opening and closing times of interval i, in hours on the same day (0 <= open[i] < close[i] <= 24). The store is open during [open[i], close[i]). Implement isOpen(int t) that returns whether the store is open at hour t.

Example 1
Input: open = [9, 14], close = [12, 18], t = 10
Output: true
Explanation: 10 is inside [9, 12).
Example 2
Input: open = [9, 14], close = [12, 18], t = 13
Output: false
Explanation: 13 is in the gap between 12 and 14. t = 12 is also false (half-open). t = 18 is false.

Constraints

  • 1 <= open.length == close.length <= 100
  • 0 <= t <= 24
  • Intervals may overlap; treat the store as open if t falls in any interval.
questions.answer:
Problem: Given open/close time arrays, check if store is open at time T.

Idea: for each interval [open[i], close[i]) (clarify inclusive bounds), test membership. Or merge intervals then binary search.

Discuss midnight wrap-around if close < open (overnight hours).

solutions.label: C++

questions.hint: Given arrays of open and close times, check if store is open at a given time T.
